text:
🇲🇽🏭 <u>US TRADE PRESSURE BITES: AUTO EXPORTS FALL 9.7% IN JULY</u>

Mexico's light-vehicle exports dropped 9.69% in July and production fell 2.2%, INEGI data shows, as trade tensions with Washington and T-MEC uncertainty hit the industry's most US-dependent sector. Year-to-date exports hold at 1.95 million vehicles, just 0.26% below 2025.

The strongest argument yet for what Mexico is already doing: diversifying markets so no single buyer can weaponize access.

🇲🇽🛒 <u>SUPERISSSTE RISES FROM THE NEOLIBERAL GRAVEYARD</u>

The state store chain decades of austerity left to rot just posted a 206% increase in sales compared to 2024.

ISSSTE director Martí Batres announced new SUPERISSSTE stores and expanded products to support workers' families — part of the Second Floor of the Fourth Transformation. What neoliberalism gutted, the 4T is rebuilding, store by store.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>SHEINBAUM TO SALAZAR: THE MAYO ZAMBADA TRANSFER IS NOT "WATER UNDER THE BRIDGE"</u>

Ex-ambassador Ken Salazar wants Mexico to "leave behind" the illegal transfer of Ismael Mayo Zambada to the United States. The President's answer:

"When there is interference by a country — in particular the United States toward Mexico, or probable interference — it's not a matter of saying: well, it's over, nothing happened." For the people of Mexico, she added, it is indispensable that everything be clarified.

A violation of sovereignty doesn't expire.

🇲🇽🎓 <u>THE REAL UNAM CHEATS AREN'T THE STUDENTS</u>

Contralínea asks the question the headline-hunters won't touch: who are the real cheaters at UNAM?

Not the kids who gamed an online exam — but the meritocracy narrative itself, when the admission exam works as an instrument of exclusion; the rector and university elites who are the exam's real deciders; a full-time faculty hiring system rigged by dedazos; and an antidemocratic university government.

The scandal was never about 3,200 exams. It's about who the exam is designed to keep out.

🇲🇽💵 <u>MEXICO TIGHTENS THE NET ON CARTEL MONEY</u>

Hacienda just published new general rules of the anti-money laundering law in the DOF: every business in "vulnerable activities" must identify the real persons behind each operation, run automated risk-detection systems, keep internal compliance manuals based on the National Risk Assessment — and pass an annual external audit. In force November 30.

While Washington points fingers, Mexico builds the legal machinery to actually choke off illicit finance.

🇲🇽🥑 <u>US BACKS DOWN: AVOCADO EXPORTS RESUME IN MICHOACÁN</u>

Washington suspended its avocado inspections in Michoacán on Wednesday, citing a security alert. By Friday it was walking it back: official activities resume this Saturday in Tancítaro, Tacámbaro, Uruapan and the Morelia-Pátzcuaro corridor — the result, the US embassy itself said, of "continuous security coordination with Mexico."

The world's avocado powerhouse doesn't stop for anyone's theater. Mexico strengthened security, kept its word, and the fruit moves north again.

🇲🇽🛢️ <u>PEMEX AND PETROBRAS NEGOTIATE SECOND DEAL: REFINING, FUELS, BIOFUELS</u>

Pemex and Brazil's Petrobras are negotiating a second cooperation agreement — refining, fuel commercialization and biofuels — Petrobras CEO Magda Chambriard confirmed, El Financiero reports. It builds on June's MOU for joint exploration in the Gulf of Mexico and extends into petrochemicals, ethanol, biodiesel and energy efficiency. Two state oil giants deepening South-South energy integration.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>VERACRUZ STRIPS IMMUNITY FROM MC MAYOR ACCUSED OF ORDERING JOURNALIST'S MURDER</u>

Veracruz's Congress voted 40-8 to remove immunity from Raúl González Martínez, the Movimiento Ciudadano mayor of Ixhuatlán del Sureste, accused as the intellectual author of the June 2 murder of journalist Roxana Berenice Guzmán Ramírez in Nanchital. He is the second MC mayor stripped of immunity in the state this week. MC calls it "political persecution" — while claiming zero tolerance for impunity.
